questions.statement: Choose the correct form of 'have' for a second conditional sentence.
questions.context: If I (have) more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.

options.text: If I had more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had' is the past of 'have' used in the if clause of a second conditional, which describes an unreal present situation.

options.text: If I have more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
options.feedback: 'If I have' describes a real present situation, so it would require the present conditional rather than 'would' in the main clause.

options.text: If I would have more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
options.feedback: 'If I would have' mixes a modal with the past of 'have' and is not the form an if clause takes.

options.text: If I having more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
options.feedback: 'If I having' needs the -ing form only after 'be', so the clause would have to be written as 'if I were having'.

questions.explanation:
The second conditional describes an imaginary or unlikely present situation. Its two halves are 'if' plus the past simple and 'would' plus the base form: if I were rich, I would travel.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the second conditional with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
questions.context: If she (study) harder, she would pass the exam.

options.text: If she study harder, she would pass the exam.
options.feedback: 'Study' has no ending, but the past simple of 'study' is 'studied' with the -y changed to -ied.

options.text: If she studies harder, she would pass the exam.
options.feedback: 'Studies' is the present simple, which belongs to the first conditional and describes a real possibility.

options.text: If she would study harder, she would pass the exam.
options.feedback: 'Would study' places a modal in the if clause, which is not how a second conditional is built.

options.text: If she studied harder, she would pass the exam.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Studied' is the past simple used in the if clause of a second conditional, and 'would pass' completes the pattern.

questions.explanation:
In a second conditional the if clause carries the past simple and the main clause carries 'would' plus the base form. The whole sentence describes a situation that is imagined rather than real.

questions.statement: Choose the correct form to complete a third conditional sentence.
questions.context: If I had known about the exam, I (would study) much more.

options.text: If I knew about the exam, I would have studied much more.
options.feedback: 'Knew' is the past simple and belongs to the second conditional, which talks about the present or the future.

options.text: If I had known about the exam, I would have studied much more.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had known' and 'would have studied' are the two halves of a third conditional, which describes an unreal situation in the past.

options.text: If I had known about the exam, I would study much more.
options.feedback: 'Would study' is the second conditional main clause; the third conditional requires 'would have' plus the past participle.

options.text: If I have known about the exam, I would have studied much more.
options.feedback: 'Have known' is a present perfect and cannot appear in the if clause of a third conditional.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional describes an unreal past situation: if I had known, I would have acted differently. Its two halves are 'if' plus 'had' plus the past participle and 'would have' plus the past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the first conditional with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
questions.context: If we (take) an umbrella, we won't get wet.

options.text: If we had taken an umbrella, we wouldn't have got wet.
options.feedback: 'Had taken' with 'wouldn't have got' is the third conditional, which describes an unreal situation in the past.

options.text: If we took an umbrella, we wouldn't get wet.
options.feedback: 'Took' with 'wouldn't get' belongs to the second conditional, which describes an unlikely present situation.

options.text: If we take an umbrella, we won't get wet.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Take' in the present simple and 'won't get' in the main clause form a first conditional about a real future possibility.

options.text: If we would take an umbrella, we wouldn't get wet.
options.feedback: 'Would take' places a modal in the if clause, which does not happen in a first conditional.

questions.explanation:
The first conditional describes a real and possible future situation: if it rains, we will stay at home. It uses the present simple in the if clause and 'will' plus the base form in the main clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the second conditional with the correct form of the verb 'be'.
questions.context: If I (be) taller, I could play basketball professionally.

options.text: If I were taller, I could play basketball professionally.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Were' is the past subjunctive used in the if clause of a second conditional, matching 'could' in the main clause.

options.text: If I am taller, I could play basketball professionally.
options.feedback: 'Am' is the present form of 'be'; a second conditional needs the past form because it describes an imaginary situation.

options.text: If I will be taller, I could play basketball professionally.
options.feedback: 'Will be' is a future form and belongs with 'will' or 'shall' in the main clause, not with 'could' in an if clause.

options.text: If I being taller, I could play basketball professionally.
options.feedback: 'Being' needs an auxiliary before it, so the clause cannot open with 'if I being'.

questions.explanation:
In a second conditional, the verb 'to be' in the if clause takes 'were' for every person: if I were you, if she were here, if they were cheaper. This 'were' is often called the subjunctive and it survives in modern English mainly in conditionals and wishes.

questions.statement: Complete the third conditional with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
questions.context: If they had left earlier, they (would catch) the train to Quito.

options.text: If they had left earlier, they would catch the train to Quito.
options.feedback: 'Would catch' is the main clause of a second conditional; the third conditional requires 'would have' plus the participle.

options.text: If they left earlier, they would have caught the train to Quito.
options.feedback: 'Left' is the past simple and belongs to the second conditional, not to a situation in the past.

options.text: If they had left earlier, they would have caught the train to Quito.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had left' and 'would have caught' are the two halves of a third conditional, and 'catch' has the irregular participle 'caught'.

options.text: If they had been leave earlier, they would have caught the train to Quito.
options.feedback: 'Had been leave' uses a participle after 'been' where the third conditional needs the past simple of 'leave', which is 'left'.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional describes what would have happened under a different past condition. Irregular verbs change their participle in this structure, so 'catch' becomes 'caught' in 'would have caught'.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly completes a question in the second conditional.
questions.context: Would you help me if I (ask) you politely?

options.text: Would you help me if I asking you politely?
options.feedback: 'Asking' needs the auxiliary 'were' before it, so the clause would be written as 'if I were asking'.

options.text: Would you help me if I ask you politely?
options.feedback: 'Ask' is the present simple and belongs to the first conditional, which describes a real situation.

options.text: Would you help me if I would ask you politely?
options.feedback: 'Would ask' places a modal in the if clause, which is not part of the conditional structure.

options.text: Would you help me if I asked you politely?
options.feedback: Correct! 'Asked' is the past simple of the if clause and 'would help' is the main clause of the second conditional.

questions.explanation:
A question in the second conditional keeps the same two halves as a statement: 'would' plus the base form in the main clause and the past simple in the if clause. Only the question mark distinguishes it.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a mixed conditional.
questions.context: If I had studied medicine, I (would work) in a hospital now.

options.text: If I studied medicine, I would have worked in a hospital now.
options.feedback: 'Studied' with 'would have worked' would make the consequence also a past event, producing a third conditional.

options.text: If I had studied medicine, I would work in a hospital now.
options.feedback: Correct! The condition is in the past and the consequence is in the present, which is the mixed conditional.

options.text: If I have studied medicine, I would work in a hospital now.
options.feedback: 'Have studied' is a present perfect and cannot describe the unreal condition of a mixed conditional.

options.text: If I had studied medicine, I would worked in a hospital now.
options.feedback: 'Would worked' mixes the modal with a past form of the verb, which never happens in English.

questions.explanation:
A mixed conditional links an unreal past condition with a present or future consequence: if I had studied, I would work there now. If I had studied, I would have worked there. The first speaks about the present, the second about the past.
---

questions.statement: Complete the third conditional negative with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
questions.context: If she hadn't slept so late, she (would not miss) the first lecture.

options.text: If she hadn't slept so late, she wouldn't have missed the first lecture.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Hadn't slept' negates the past condition and 'wouldn't have missed' negates the past consequence with the participle.

options.text: If she didn't sleep so late, she wouldn't have missed the first lecture.
options.feedback: 'Didn't sleep' is a first conditional condition, which does not match 'wouldn't have missed' in the main clause.

options.text: If she hadn't slept so late, she wouldn't miss the first lecture.
options.feedback: 'Wouldn't miss' is a second conditional consequence; the third conditional requires 'wouldn't have' plus the participle.

options.text: If she hadn't slept so late, she wouldn't have miss the first lecture.
options.feedback: 'Wouldn't have miss' uses the base form after 'have'; that construction needs the past participle 'missed'.

questions.explanation:
A negative third conditional negates both halves independently: if it hadn't rained, we wouldn't have gone. Each half keeps its own auxiliary, 'hadn't' in the condition and 'wouldn't have' in the consequence.

questions.statement: Complete the second conditional with the correct form of the verb 'know'.
questions.context: I don't know where she is. If I (know), I would tell you.

options.text: If I know, I would tell you where she is.
options.feedback: 'Know' is the present simple, which would require 'will tell' rather than 'would tell' in the main clause.

options.text: If I knew, I would tell you where she is.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Knew' is the past simple in the if clause and 'would tell' completes the second conditional pattern.

options.text: If I would know, I would tell you where she is.
options.feedback: 'Would know' places a modal in the if clause, which is not part of the conditional structure.

options.text: If I have known, I would tell you where she is.
options.feedback: 'Have known' is a present perfect and describes something that happened before a past moment, not an unreal present situation.

questions.explanation:
Second conditional sentences of this kind describe what would be possible if the speaker had the information they lack. The past simple in the if clause creates that distance from reality.

options.feedback: 'Erupts' is the present simple and belongs to the first conditional, which describes a real possibility.

options.feedback: 'Would erupt' places a modal in the if clause, which does not occur in a second conditional.

options.text: If the volcano erupted again, the town would have to be evacuated.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Erupted' is the past simple in the if clause and 'would have to' completes the second conditional.

questions.explanation:
A second conditional about a serious risk uses the past simple to place the event outside the realm of certainty: if it erupted, we would evacuate. The main clause then carries 'would' plus the base form.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly completes the third conditional.
questions.context: If you had backed up your files, you (would not lose) all your work.

options.text: If you had backed up your files, you would not lose all your work.
options.feedback: 'Would not lose' has no 'have', so the consequence is not placed in the past as a third conditional requires.

options.text: If you backed up your files, you would not lose all your work.
options.feedback: 'Backed up' is the past simple and 'would not lose' is a second conditional, so the sentence describes the present instead of the past.

options.text: If you had backed up your files, you would not have lost all your work.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had backed up' is the past perfect condition and 'would not have lost' is the negative third conditional consequence.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional is used for regrets about the past: if you had studied, you would have passed. Both halves refer to the past, and neither uses the present simple form of the verb.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'have' in a second conditional.
questions.context: If I had a car, I would drive to work instead of taking the bus.

options.text: If I had a car, I would drive to work instead of taking the bus.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had' is the past of 'have' in the if clause and 'would drive' completes the second conditional.

options.text: If I would have a car, I would drive to work instead of taking the bus.
options.feedback: 'Would have' places a modal in the if clause, which is not how a conditional is formed.

questions.explanation:
The verb 'have' behaves like any other verb in a second conditional: it takes the past simple 'had' in the if clause and the main clause carries 'would' plus the base form.

options.text: If the rain had not fall yesterday, we could have gone to the park.
options.feedback: 'Had not fall' uses the base form after 'had not'; that construction needs the past participle.

options.text: If the rain did not fall yesterday, we could have gone to the park.
options.feedback: 'Did not fall' is a first conditional condition and does not match 'could have gone' in the main clause.

options.text: If the rain had not fallen yesterday, we could have gone to the park.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had not fallen' is the negative past perfect condition, and 'could have gone' is the third conditional consequence.

options.text: If the rain had not been fallen yesterday, we could have gone to the park.
options.feedback: 'Had not been fallen' uses the passive after 'been' where the third conditional needs the active past participle 'fallen'.

questions.explanation:
A negative third conditional places 'not' after the auxiliary: if it had not rained, we would have gone. The verb still needs its past participle, so 'had not rained' rather than 'had not rain'.

questions.context: Where would you live if you (win) the lottery?

options.text: Where would you live if you won the lottery?

options.feedback: 'Would improved' adds a past form after the modal, which never happens in English.

questions.statement: Complete the mixed conditional with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
questions.context: If they hadn't missed the last bus, they (would not be) walking home in the dark.

options.text: If they hadn't missed the bus, they would not be walking home in the dark.
options.feedback: Correct! The condition is an unreal past event and the consequence is a present state, which is the mixed conditional.

options.text: If they didn't miss the bus, they would not be walking home in the dark.
options.feedback: 'Didn't miss' is a first conditional condition and does not match the past perfect needed here.

options.text: If they hadn't missed the bus, they would not walking home in the dark.
options.feedback: 'Would not walking' is missing the auxiliary 'be' that a continuous form requires.

options.feedback: 'Had been miss' uses a participle after 'been' where the third conditional needs the past simple 'missed'.

questions.explanation:
A mixed conditional has 'if' plus 'had' plus the past participle for the condition and 'would' plus an ordinary present form for the consequence. It often describes a situation that is still true at the moment of speaking.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly advises using the second conditional.
questions.context: If I were you, I would apologise and explain the mistake honestly.

options.text: If I was you, I would apologise and explain the mistake honestly.
options.feedback: 'Was' is the past simple, but this fixed expression always uses the subjunctive 'were'.

options.text: If I were you, I would apologise and explain the mistake honestly.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Were' belongs to the formula 'if I were you' and 'would apologise' completes the second conditional.

options.text: If I were you, I would to apologise and explain the mistake honestly.
options.feedback: 'Would to apologise' adds an infinitive marker that never follows a modal verb.

The expression 'if I were you' is one of the standard ways of giving advice in English. The subjunctive 'were' appears with every person of the pronoun, which is the clearest surviving use of that mood.

questions.statement: Complete the second conditional with the correct form of the verb 'be'.
questions.context: If the shop (be) open on Sunday, we would buy the tickets there.

options.text: If the shop will be open on Sunday, we would buy the tickets there.
options.feedback: 'Will be' is a future form and belongs with 'will' in the main clause, not with 'would' in an if clause.

options.text: If the shop are open on Sunday, we would buy the tickets there.
options.feedback: 'Are' is the plural present form and does not agree with the singular subject 'the shop'.

options.text: If the shop be open on Sunday, we would buy the tickets there.
options.feedback: 'Be' is the bare infinitive and needs a past form before it in a second conditional if clause.

options.text: If the shop were open on Sunday, we would buy the tickets there.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Were' is the past subjunctive used with the singular subject 'the shop' in a second conditional if clause.

questions.explanation:
In the if clause of a second conditional, 'to be' takes the form 'were' with every subject: if the shop were open, if I were you, if they were cheaper. This is the standard rule in written English.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a mixed third and second conditional.
questions.context: We did not get the job, but if she (have) asked for more experience, she might have got it.

options.text: If she had asked for more experience, she might got the job.
options.feedback: 'Might got' lacks the 'have' that the modal perfect requires after 'might'.

options.text: If she has asked for more experience, she might have got the job.
options.feedback: 'Has asked' is a present perfect and cannot appear in the if clause of a third conditional.

options.text: If she had asked for more experience, she might have got the job.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Had asked' is the third conditional condition and 'might have got' is its consequence, also in the past.

options.text: If she had been asked for more experience, she might have got the job.
options.feedback: 'Had been asked' is the passive, which would mean somebody else asked her rather than her asking herself.

questions.explanation:
'Might have' plus a past participle is the modal third conditional. It expresses a past possibility that did not happen, and it combines freely with 'could have', 'would have' and 'should have'.
